name: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
title: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
answer: Agent negotiation in over the counter markets covers software agents that represent buyers, sellers, dealers, or clients in bilateral and voice or chat based trading of instruments not listed on exchanges, such as swaps, bonds, FX forwards, and structured notes. It sits within agent workflows in finance because the agent must quote, counterquote, check credit and inventory, and reach a tradeable agreement rather than simply route an order. The scope includes request for quote workflows, streaming prices, and multi dealer negotiation, and it overlaps with electronic trading, market making, and post trade processing. It does not cover exchange traded order books or retail brokerage apps except where they connect to over the counter liquidity.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Agent negotiation in over the counter markets covers software agents that represent buyers, sellers, dealers, or clients in bilateral and voice or chat based trading of instruments not listed on exchanges, such as swaps, bonds, FX forwards, and structured notes. It sits within agent workflows in finance because the agent must quote, counterquote, check credit and inventory, and reach a tradeable agreement rather than simply route an order. The scope includes request for quote workflows, streaming prices, and multi dealer negotiation, and it overlaps with electronic trading, market making, and post trade processing. It does not cover exchange traded order books or retail brokerage apps except where they connect to over the counter liquidity.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The agents run on trading desks and dealer platforms, connected to pricing engines, risk systems, order management systems, and chat or voice gateways. They need low latency market data, credit limits, inventory positions, and legal entity identifiers, plus audit logs that record every quote and message. Common building blocks include FIX and other messaging protocols, application programming interfaces to electronic venues, and natural language models for parsing chat or email negotiations. Because over the counter markets are bilateral, the infrastructure often spans multiple firms, so identity, permissions, and data sharing agreements matter as much as compute.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A negotiation agent typically starts from a client request or a dealer quote, then uses a policy to propose price and size, respond to counteroffers, and decide when to accept, reject, or escalate to a human. The policy may combine game theoretic bargaining, reinforcement learning from historical trades, and rules that enforce credit, regulatory, and inventory constraints. Natural language models can read unstructured messages and draft replies, while a separate execution layer checks the final terms against limits before sending. Human traders often set guardrails, review exceptions, and handle relationship sensitive or complex trades.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Firms need clear records of who authorized an agent, what data trained it, and which messages led to a trade, because over the counter negotiations can create binding obligations and disputes. Risk controls include pre trade credit checks, kill switches, message surveillance, and reconciliation with legal confirmations, and compliance teams map agent behavior to market conduct rules. Provenance covers the source of pricing data, the version of the model, and the chain of custody for chat and voice transcripts. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, a sign of how much attention these controls receive, though specific obligations depend on jurisdiction and instrument. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more agents that negotiate across multiple dealers and asset classes, with humans moving to oversight of exceptions and relationship management. Standardization of negotiation protocols, audit trails, and model documentation will likely matter more than raw model capability, because over the counter markets reward trust and enforceable terms. Adoption may be fastest in liquid, electronic segments such as FX and rates, and slower in bespoke credit and structured products where terms are unique. The direction is toward hybrid desks where agents handle routine quotes and humans own complex, relationship driven, or disputed negotiations.
